source.title: Safety of Antiseizure Medications During Direct Oral Anticoagulant Therapy in Epilepsy

Objective.canonical_statement: The study compared thromboembolic events, major bleeding, and all-cause mortality across commonly used antiseizure medications in adults with epilepsy receiving direct oral anticoagulants.

Design, Setting, and Participants.canonical_statement: The investigators used a retrospective cohort design that emulated a target trial for each antiseizure medication group against an active comparator, with 1:1 propensity score matching in four cohorts to estimate a sustained-monotherapy per-protocol outcome.
Participant data came from the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network, a federated deidentified electronic health record network spanning 165 health care organizations internationally.

Adults aged 18 years or older with epilepsy were eligible; the abstract reports exclusions for recent vitamin K antagonist use, strong non-antiseizure CYP3A4/P-glycoprotein modulators, and major vascular events in the prior year.
Participant follow-up began at a prespecified 90-day landmark, and the reported analyses were performed from January through March 2026.

Exposures.canonical_statement: The exposure groups were levetiracetam, valproate, moderate enzyme-inducing antiseizure medications, and strong enzyme-inducing antiseizure medications, each evaluated during monotherapy.
Lamotrigine or lacosamide formed one pooled active-comparator reference group.

Main Outcomes and Measures.canonical_statement: The primary thromboembolic composite included ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, and systemic or peripheral embolism.
Major bleeding was a primary outcome.
All-cause mortality was a primary outcome.

Results.canonical_statement: Of 2.29 million adults with epilepsy, 40,932 were DOAC eligible, 26,962 had DOAC-antiseizure medication overlap within 6 months, 10,209 were monotherapy eligible, and 9,529 initiators formed the analytic cohort.
The analytic cohort contained 9,529 initiators with mean age 63 years (SD 18); 4,869 participants (51%) were female.
Levetiracetam initiators numbered 5,473 participants (57% of the analytic cohort).
Strong enzyme-inducing ASM initiators numbered 1,395 participants (15% of the analytic cohort).
Valproate initiators numbered 1,006 participants (11% of the analytic cohort).
Moderate enzyme-inducing ASM initiators numbered 382 participants (4% of the analytic cohort).
Compared with lamotrigine/lacosamide, levetiracetam was associated with higher thromboembolic risk (HR 1.98, 95% CI 1.37 to 2.87).
Compared with lamotrigine/lacosamide, levetiracetam was associated with higher all-cause mortality (HR 1.60, 95% CI 1.23 to 2.08).
Compared with lamotrigine/lacosamide, strong enzyme-inducing antiseizure medications were associated with higher thromboembolic risk (HR 1.55, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.36).
Compared with lamotrigine/lacosamide, strong enzyme-inducing antiseizure medications were associated with lower major bleeding risk (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.83).
Compared with lamotrigine/lacosamide, valproate was associated with higher all-cause mortality (HR 1.49, 95% CI 1.09 to 2.04).
Compared with lamotrigine/lacosamide, valproate was associated with higher intracranial major bleeding risk (HR 3.01, 95% CI 1.45 to 6.26).
The abstract reports comparable major bleeding risk for levetiracetam versus lamotrigine/lacosamide, without an effect estimate in the accessible abstract.
The abstract reports that approximately 28% of thromboembolic events were potentially preventable under a lamotrigine/lacosamide reference.
In a sensitivity analysis of vitamin K antagonist-treated adults, the abstract reports thromboembolic risks as near null.

Conclusions and Relevance.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that antiseizure medication selection was associated with distinct thromboembolic, bleeding, and mortality risks in adults with epilepsy receiving DOACs and may represent a modifiable contributor to clinical outcomes.
